court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: The plaintiff's furnished-room and boarding income appears only as economic background to a dispute over an alleged partnership and illicit cohabitation agreement; the court did not adjudicate the boarders' occupancy.
The case concerns regulation of fat rendering as a public nuisance, not compensated occupancy or lodging.
The occupancy at issue was a former owner's continued possession of an entire factory, not dwelling, room, boarding, or lodging occupancy.

holding_summary: The court affirmed recovery for breach of an oral agreement for rooms, board, and attendance because the defendant waived the Statute of Frauds by failing to plead it. The court expressly declined to decide whether the arrangement constituted a lease rather than a contract for board and lodging.

quotes.text: The conclusion is thus reached that the defendant waived the benefit of the statute in this case by omitting to plead it.

notes: The plaintiff was a lessee who conducted the arrangement in the house described as her home and business. Characterization is null because the court stated that it was unnecessary to decide whether the agreement was a lease or a board-and-lodging contract.
The rented room was factual background to a murder prosecution; payment, the room provider, and the legal character of the occupancy were not adjudicated.
The case concerns fire-safety regulation of packing-box storage in a commercial yard, not lodging or compensated room occupancy.

cite: Adams v. New Jersey Steamboat Co., 151 N.Y. 163
holding_summary: A steamboat company furnishing a paid private stateroom was subject to the common-law responsibility of an innkeeper. It was liable without proof of negligence for reasonable traveling money stolen from the passenger's locked stateroom when the passenger was not negligent.

quotes.text: A steamer carrying passengers upon the water, and furnishing them with rooms and entertainment, is, for all practical purposes, a floating inn, and hence the duties which the proprietors owe to the passengers in their charge ought to be the same.
We are of the opinion, therefore, that the defendant was properly held liable in this case for the money stolen from the plaintiff without any proof of negligence.
The passenger procures and pays for his room for the same reasons that a guest at an inn does.

notes: The occupancy was one overnight journey in a paid stateroom; the case protects the short-term occupant through an innkeeper-like liability rule.
The case concerns a tenant's ownership and removal of fixtures, not compensated dwelling or room occupancy.
The case defines a qualified agricultural right of way and contains no compensated occupancy or lodging issue.

cite: Adams v. New Jersey Steamboat Co., 9 Misc. 25
court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The court affirmed application of an innkeeper-like liability rule to a steamboat company that assigned a passenger a stateroom. Proof that reasonable traveling money was lost from the room without the passenger's contributory negligence established a prima facie case without proof of the company's negligence.

quotes.text: where it was held that a liability, analogous to that of an innkeeper, attached to the class of carriers to which this defendant belongs, with regard to a loss of personal effects taken into his stateroom by the passenger.

The rule referred to was, in effect, that the defendant company was liable for the loss of plaintiff’s money, to an amount which might reasonably be carried for traveling expenses, retained by him in his designated stateroom, without proof of negligence upon the part of defendant, and that, upon showing that the loss occurred without contributory negligence on his own part, plaintiff established a grima facie case, the contract of carriage and the assignment of the stateroom in question being undisputed.
There was sufficient evidence in the case to justify a submission of the question of plaintiff’s contributory negligence to the jury, and the verdict is to be supported.

notes: The paid occupancy lasted one night aboard the steamboat; the decision was later affirmed at 151 N.Y. 163.
The licensing dispute concerns a place of public amusement, not a lodging or boarding establishment.

cite: People ex rel. Cairns v. Murray, 13 Misc. 522
notes: The case concerns a liquor license for an established saloon; its references to hotels are statutory exceptions rather than adjudication of lodging occupancy.
Keeping boarders was evidence about whether possession gave notice of an unrecorded deed, but the court did not adjudicate the boarders' rights, occupancy, or regulation.

holding_summary: The court held that when spouses lived together and the wife kept boarders in their house, the husband was entitled to the board money unless a special agreement made it the wife's separate property. Refusal to give that instruction required reversal and a new trial.

quotes.text: The evidence shows that the defendant was a married man during the period aforesaid, and tended to show that he kept house, and that the plaintiff lived in the family and that his board and lodging was worth three dollars per week.'

At the close of this case defendant’s counsel asked the court to charge that where husband and wife lived together, and the wife kept boarders, and the boarders are kept in the house, that the husband is entitled to the money paid for board, unless a special agreement is shown between the husband and wife, allowing the wife to have that claim for her sole • property.
We think this was-error; the defendant was entitled to have the proposition charged* as requested, and we cannot say that the refusal did not prejudice the defendant.

notes: The occupancy ran from August 1884 to March 1890 and occurred within the married couple's household. Polarity reflects judicial recognition and enforcement of the household boarding claim, notwithstanding the marital-property rule allocating the money to the husband.
